record_type_quote: The replication attempt was conducted in an existing dataset similar to the dataset used in the original report, by a team of independent investigators in consultation with the original authors.

targets.title: Brain connectomics predict response to treatment in social anxiety disorder.
targets.evidence_quote: Here, we conducted an independent replication of a previous report that response to cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for social anxiety disorder (SAD) could be accurately predicted from baseline brain connectivity
targets.outcome_quote: We tested the precise model developed in the original report. This model provided a small improvement in the prediction of treatment response. It explained an additional 2% of the variance beyond baseline symptom severity, which attained marginal statistical significance and was approximately 1/10th of the effect size in the original report. A more flexible test of model replication, which used the amygdala connectivity target regions from the original report and estimated model parameters on the replication dataset, found no significant prediction of treatment response.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors describe positive prediction with the precise model but no significant prediction with the more flexible replication and no prediction in the immediate-treatment subset. Mixed rests on that contrast, not on effect-size shrinkage alone. Their overall support for some amygdala features is broader than confirmation of the particular original model; marginal significance makes the positive comparison uncertain. Underpowering is discussed without an explicit verdict that this attempt cannot adjudicate.

reasoning: A different patient sample, already collected, is used to test the published prediction model. This is replication rather than reproduction. Reference 1 identifies the sole target; other amygdala models and papers supplying the new dataset are not targets.
